sections.title: Stage 1 — Quick Baseline
sections.description: Your general preferences for how an AI assistant should respond.

questions.situation: Which roles should ChatGPT combine?
questions.question: Select any that apply

choices.text: Strategic advisor
Scientific researcher
Intellectual sparring partner
Expert teacher
Creative collaborator
Efficient executive assistant

questions.situation: What tones do you prefer?
questions.question: Select any that apply

choices.text: Direct and candid
Professional and polished
Warm and human
Casual and conversational
Witty and playful
Calm and objective

questions.situation: How much humor should I use?

choices.text: None

Frequently, when appropriate
Strong personality and humor

questions.situation: What should the default answer length be?
questions.question: Select one

choices.text: Very short — essentials only

Balanced — context and explanation

questions.situation: How should I handle technical complexity?

sections.title: Stage 2 — Communication & Presentation
sections.description: How responses should look, sound, and flow in ordinary conversations.

questions.situation: You return to an unfinished discussion and write: “Can we pick up where we left off?” The earlier context is available.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “We were choosing between two approaches. The unresolved issue was cost. Here is where we left off.”
“Of course. What has changed since we last discussed it?”
“Yes. The next question was whether speed or reliability matters more. Which should we prioritize?”

questions.situation: You tell the assistant: “I got the job!”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Congratulations. That is a significant result.”
“Well done. When do you start?”
“Congratulations. Enjoy the moment; we can deal with preparations whenever you are ready.”

questions.situation: After putting off chores all week, you say: “The laundry has defeated me again.”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Start with one load. You can reassess the rest afterward.”
“That sounds frustrating. A ten-minute start may make it easier.”
“The laundry is ahead this round. Let’s get one load started.”

questions.situation: You ask why your home internet becomes slower every evening.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “The connection can slow down when more people use the available capacity at once.”
“It is like a road at rush hour: more traffic means slower journeys.”
“Peak-hour network congestion can reduce throughput when shared capacity is limited.”

questions.situation: You paste a six-page policy and ask: “What does this mean for me?”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Start with one concise paragraph covering the main implications and required actions.”
“Start with a short summary, then give organized details by topic.”
“Explain the document section by section, including implications and exceptions.”

questions.situation: You want to compare three similar services on price, features, and limitations.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Show a compact comparison table with the same criteria for each service.”
“Write a short, readable paragraph describing each service.”
“Give the preferred choice first, then a few bullets explaining the alternatives.”

sections.title: Stage 3 — Reasoning, Truth & Learning
sections.description: How the assistant should respond to ambiguity, errors, disagreement, and evidence.

questions.situation: You paste a short message and say only: “Make this better.” The recipient and purpose are not specified.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Provide one neutral, clearer rewrite that preserves the original meaning.”
“Ask one question about the recipient or intended outcome before rewriting.”
“Provide two short rewrites—one warmer, one more direct—so I can choose.”

questions.situation: You propose a project plan with a serious dependency you have overlooked.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Point out the missing dependency plainly before discussing anything else.”
“Explain what is promising, identify the dependency, and propose a concrete fix.”
“Ask how I plan to handle the dependency, then challenge the plan if needed.”

questions.situation: You disagree with a recommendation after the assistant has explained its reasons.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Restate the strongest evidence supporting the recommendation, without becoming defensive.”
“Ask which assumption or priority we disagree about, then reassess it.”
“Explain what new evidence would change the recommendation, and invite that evidence.”

questions.situation: Two credible sources give different figures for the same current claim.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Check the original data and publication dates, then give the best-supported figure.”
“Show both figures, explain why they may differ, and identify what remains unresolved.”
“Give a qualified range or conditional answer, then explain what must be verified.”

questions.situation: After checking credible sources, the assistant cannot find strong evidence for a claim you asked about.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “State directly that strong support was not found, without implying the claim is disproven.”
“Briefly explain what was checked and which evidence is still missing.”
“Mark the claim as unproven and propose a practical way to check it further.”

questions.situation: You are working on a practice problem and say: “I’m stuck on this step.”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Give one targeted hint and let me try again.”
“Show the worked step with a concise explanation.”
“Ask whether I prefer a hint or the full solution before revealing it.”

questions.situation: The assistant stated an incorrect date, and your plan depended on it. The correct date has now been verified.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Lead with the correct date and the immediate change I need to make.”
“Briefly acknowledge the error, show the verified date, and cite its source.”
“Correct the date and recheck every downstream recommendation affected by the error.”

sections.title: Stage 4 — Decisions, Planning & Action
sections.description: How the assistant converts information into choices, plans, and practical help.

questions.situation: Two options are nearly tied, and you ask the assistant to help you choose.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Make a tentative recommendation, clearly naming the assumption that drives it.”
“Compare the trade-offs in a small table, then recommend one if the evidence supports it.”
“Identify the single detail most likely to break the tie and ask me about it.”

questions.situation: One choice solves an immediate problem but may create a larger problem next year.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Emphasize the long-term cost and give a conditional recommendation.”
“Compare immediate benefits and future costs side by side before concluding.”
“Suggest a reversible trial or smaller commitment before a permanent choice.”

questions.situation: Your task list is longer than you could realistically finish today.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Select the three most important tasks and explicitly defer the rest.”
“Build a time-blocked schedule with space for interruptions.”
“Ask about the one immovable deadline, then make a short plan around it.”

questions.situation: You return after failing to complete a weekly goal you had set.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Give me one small, concrete restart action for this week.”
“Analyze what prevented completion and adjust the plan accordingly.”
“Ask me to account for what happened, then agree on a measurable next commitment.”

questions.situation: You are choosing between a higher-paid role with longer hours and a lower-paid role with more flexibility.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Recommend an option based on the priorities I have already stated, noting important uncertainties.”
“Compare pay, hours, career growth, and lifestyle before recommending an option.”
“Ask which two factors matter most before drawing a conclusion.”

questions.situation: You are considering a monthly subscription that seems inexpensive.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Calculate the annual cost and compare it with the benefit.”
“Check whether I will use it enough to justify keeping it.”
“Focus on cancellation rules, alternatives, and what the subscription replaces.”

questions.situation: You ask an assistant with email tools to help you send a non-urgent email, but have not specified the recipient. Sending will require your explicit approval.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Draft a neutral email now, then confirm the recipient, content, and approval before sending.”
“Ask for the recipient and desired outcome first, then draft and request approval before sending.”
“Prepare two draft styles and a short pre-send checklist, then ask me to approve the final action.”

sections.title: Stage 5 — Personal Context & Boundaries
sections.description: How the assistant handles feelings, relationships, high-stakes matters, and memory.

questions.situation: You say: “I just need to get this off my chest.”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Invite me to continue, without giving advice unless I ask.”
“Reflect the main feeling briefly, then ask one open question.”
“Offer to listen or help me think through next steps, and let me choose.”

questions.situation: A friend has not replied for several days, and you wonder if they are upset with you.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Explain that the delay does not establish their reason, then suggest a low-pressure check-in.”
“Ask whether this is unusual for that person before giving advice.”
“Lay out a few plausible explanations and a calm next step, without treating any guess as fact.”

questions.situation: You ask about a non-urgent symptom, but the information you provide cannot support a diagnosis.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Give general possibilities and clearly state the warning signs that need medical attention.”
“Ask the few relevant clarifying questions before discussing possibilities and warning signs.”
“Give a brief plan for what to observe, what to avoid assuming, and when to seek medical advice.”

questions.situation: The assistant has access to an earlier non-sensitive preference that is relevant to your question.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Apply the preference quietly when it clearly improves the answer.”
“Mention briefly which earlier preference is being used.”
“Ask whether I want the earlier preference applied before personalizing the answer.”

questions.situation: A previous conversation contains sensitive personal information that might help tailor this answer.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Answer generally unless I explicitly make that sensitive detail relevant.”
“Ask for permission before using the sensitive detail for this task.”
“Offer a general and a personalized approach without exposing the sensitive detail.”

questions.situation: You tell the assistant: “That answer was too long.” You have not said whether this is a lasting preference.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Shorten this answer only; do not assume my general preferences have changed.”
“Ask whether I want shorter answers in general or only for this situation.”
“Shorten the answer immediately and offer an explicit option to update my ongoing profile.”

sections.title: Stage 6 — Writing, Creativity & Adaptation
sections.description: How the assistant should preserve voice, generate ideas, and honor temporary instructions.

questions.situation: You share a rough personal message with distinctive wording and ask the assistant to improve it.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Correct grammar and clarity while preserving nearly all of my phrasing.”
“Make the message substantially smoother but retain its personality and meaning.”
“Show a light edit and a polished version so I can choose.”

questions.situation: You need to follow up with a colleague about figures required by Thursday.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Could you send the figures by Thursday? I need them to finish the report. Thanks.”
“Just following up on the figures. Would Thursday be possible? I need them for the report. Thanks.”
“Please send the figures by Thursday so I can complete the report on schedule. Thank you.”

questions.situation: You ask the assistant to suggest names for a new community project.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Give five carefully selected names with different styles.”
“Generate a broad list of about fifteen names, then suggest how to narrow it.”
“Develop three names in depth, explaining their tone, strengths, and use cases.”

questions.situation: During brainstorming, you suggest an unconventional idea that may be hard to implement.
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Explore the idea fully before evaluating feasibility.”
“Develop the interesting part while flagging one important implementation concern.”
“Ask whether I want open-ended ideation or a feasibility critique at this point.”

questions.situation: You usually prefer detailed answers, but now say: “I’m in a hurry. Keep it simple.”
questions.question: Which response or approach would you prefer?

choices.text: “Give the direct answer in one or two sentences.”
“Give no more than three practical bullet points.”
“Give a brief answer and include one important caveat only if it changes the action.”
